facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The temple shrine famous for Lord Venkateshwara receives between 50,000 and 1 lakh visitors every day, according to the TTD official website.
facts.text: According to official administrative statistics released by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, the hill shrine accommodates between 50,000 and 100,000 pilgrims on a typical day.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The first recorded endowment was made by Pallava queen Samavai in the year 966 CE.
facts.text: An epigraphical survey by the Archaeological Survey of India documented that the earliest dated inscription in the temple records the donation of land and consecration of a silver deity by Pallava queen Samavai in 966 CE.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: One significant inscription from 1019 AD, during Rajendra Chola-I's reign, mandates strict maintenance of the temple kitchen, or 'Potu,' with severe punishment for non-compliance.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Epigraphy Branch
facts.text: An inscription documented by the Archaeological Survey of India dating to the regnal year of Rajendra Chola I in 1019 CE orders an inquiry into the management of endowments and sets standards for ghee storage in the temple kitchen.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: In 1517, Vijayanagara Emperor Krishnadevaraya, on one of his many visits to the temple, donated gold and jewels, enabling the Ananda Nilayam (inner shrine) roofing to be gilded.
facts.text: Epigraphical records compiled by the Archaeological Survey of India reveal that Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya donated gold and gems to guild the Ananda Nilayam temple canopy in 1517 CE.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Mysore Archaeological Society of India (ASI) Director (Epigraphy) Dr K Munirathnam Reddy explained that around 1,150 inscriptions in Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu were found around the temple.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Epigraphy Branch
facts.text: Epigraphists from the Archaeological Survey of India cataloged approximately 1,150 historical stone inscriptions in Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada across the shrines of Tirumala and Tirupati.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The Venkatam hill is mentioned in Tamil Sangam literature dated to 300 BCE.
facts.text: Historians disagree over the era of origin of the Tirumala sanctuary, as literary scholars cite Tamil Sangam poetry from approximately 300 BCE referencing the sacred Vengadam hill, whereas material and epigraphical evidence establishes the earliest temple structure only from the medieval Pallava era.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: According to the Bhavishyottara Purana tradition, Srinivasa approached Kubera, the divine treasurer, for financial help... Kubera agreed, with repayment and interest extending through Kali Yuga.
facts.text: The Bhavishyottara Purana states that Srinivasa obtained a massive loan of wealth from Kubera to marry Padmavati and committed to repaying interest until the end of Kali Yuga.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: According to the Varaha Purana, Adi Varaha manifested himself on the western bank of the Swami Pushkarini, while Vishnu in the form of Venkateswara came in to reside on the southern bank of the Swami Pushkarini.
facts.text: The Varaha Purana relates that Adi Varaha first inhabited the western banks of Swami Pushkarini and allocated the surrounding hills of Venkatadri to Lord Venkateswara.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Śrī Venkaṭeśāth paro devo nāsthy anyoḥ śaraṇam bhuvi | Venkaṭeśa samo devo nāsti nāsti maheṭale
facts.text: The Varaha Purana states that no deity equal to Lord Venkateswara exists on Earth to grant ultimate refuge to human beings in the Kali Yuga.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Lord Venkateswara's idol is real human hair, never tangles, remains smooth.
facts.text: A widespread oral tradition asserts that the stone idol in the Tirumala sanctum possesses soft, genuine human hair that never develops tangles.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: A celestial princess named Neela Devi noticed this and immediately cut a portion of her own hair to cover the Lord's bald patch.
facts.text: A popular devotional legend states that the celestial maiden Neela Devi clipped her own locks to restore hair lost from Srinivasa's head after an injury, inspiring the tradition of pilgrim tonsure.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: If you put your ear close to the wall behind the Balaji idol, you can hear the sound of sea waves.
facts.text: A long-standing local folklore tale holds that devotees who listen closely behind the sanctum idol can hear the sound of oceanic waves.
